lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Is this fair, Pluto? Me dead at thirty, while old Thucritus over ninety is still alive?

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Absolutely fair, Terpsion. He lives without wishing any of his friends dead. You spent your whole time plotting against him, waiting for the inheritance.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Shouldn’t an old man who can’t even enjoy his wealth anymore just bow out and let the young have their turn?

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: New laws from you now, Terpsion? Anyone who can’t squeeze pleasure out of their money has to die? Fate and nature have their own rules.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Well, I blame this setup. It ought to run in order: oldest first, then the next oldest. Not this backwards business where the super-elderly hang on with three teeth left, barely seeing, hunched over four slaves, nose dripping, eyes gummy, no pleasures left at all, a living tomb everyone laughs at, while the best-looking, strongest young men drop dead. That’s upside-down. Or at least we should know exactly when each old man’s going to die, so we don’t waste our time flattering the wrong ones. As the proverb says, the cart keeps pulling the ox.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: It all works out cleverer than you think, Terpsion. What is it with you lot, slavering over other people’s money and attaching yourselves to childless old men? That’s why you get buried before them and everyone finds it hilarious. The harder you pray for them to die, the happier the world is when you go first. You’ve invented a whole new craft: chasing after old women and old men, especially the ones with no children. The ones with families are off the menu for you. But plenty of your targets catch on to the scam. If they have sons, they pretend to hate them so they can pick up lovers of their own. Then in the wills the old flatterers get cut out, nature and the son win as they should, and you’re left grinding your teeth.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: You’re right. Thucritus swallowed everything I sent him, always moaning that he was on his last legs. Every time I walked in he’d groan and whimper like a half-hatched chick. I kept thinking he’d be in the coffin any second, so I kept sending more than the other suitors, and I lay awake nights counting it all and making plans. Insomnia and worry are what killed me. And he swallowed the bait whole and stood laughing over my grave the other day.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Well done, Thucritus. Live as long as you like, rich and laughing at the lot of them. Don’t die until you’ve seen every flatterer off first.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: That’s the best thing I’ve heard, Pluto. If only Charoeades would go before Thucritus too.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Don’t worry, Terpsion. Phidon and Melanthus and all the rest will go ahead of him, with exactly the same worries.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: I like the sound of that. Live long, Thucritus.
